comment: Items are CONTENT, like materials.json and glyphs.json â€” not look-and-feel knobs like tuning.json. This file holds an item's BEHAVIOUR: its id, the kind the engine switches on, and its damage numbers. THE ART IS NOT HERE, and it is not part of any creature either: each item owns <id>.vox plus an <id>.json sidecar carrying its grip and its cutting edge. A held item BORROWS a rig slot, so while worn it is a real rig part â€” severable with the arm, droppable as debris, carvable per voxel â€” but its geometry has its own origin, so a weapon can never inflate the box of the body holding it. That was a real bug: as a rig prop the sword reached 30 micro outside mina's prefab box and drew her body offset from her own arm. Hot-reloads on R alongside materials and glyphs.
kinds: melee = swung, and cuts along the `edge` segment its own sidecar declares (see scripts/gen_sword_item.py). The blade geometry is what decides the wound; `carveBonus` only widens it. A HIT IS THREE PARTS (src/game/impact.h): `damage` is the CUT part (the key is not renamed -- it is still the honest name for the half of a blow that opens a wound), `blunt` is trauma that charges hp and bruises without ever dismembering, and `bite` is a tear (authored on creatures, not on items). `bluntCarve` and `armorBreak` are 0..1 fractions of a tuning radius -- how much of gore.bluntCarveRadius a blow dents out of flesh, and how much of gear.bluntDentRadius it breaks out of a worn shell. That is why a mace beats plate and a sword does not. container = a vessel (src/game/container.h): `container.holds` names the material CLASSES it takes up (liquid, powder), `capacity` is in cells, the rates are cells per tick, and `applyCells` is what one click on a limb in the health panel spends. The flask and the pouch are the same kind; what differs is data.

items.desc: A straight double-edged arming sword. Held point-up; it cuts with the length of its blade, so where you land it is where the wound opens.
A two-handed cleaver, wide at the tip and heavy with it. It is not quicker than a sword and it is not subtler; it simply arrives with more behind the edge, and takes a limb in a third of the blows.

Two feet of straight double-edged blade on a one-hand grip. It gives up the arming sword's last third of reach and about a third of its weight with it, and hands back a weapon you can still swing inside somebody's guard.

A hand's length of point, and barely a fifth of the sword behind it. It will not take an arm off in one pass and it was never going to; what it does is open the same wound over and over while standing closer than a sword can answer.

A flanged head on a short wrapped haft. It has almost no edge and does not want one: what it does is arrive, and a man in plate is still a man with a plate-shaped dent in him. Against an unarmoured body it bruises and caves rather than opening, so it will hammer somebody to death without ever taking an arm off.
A deep cloth cowl. It keeps the rain off and catches fire readily; what it will not do is stop a blade.
A heavy black robe, sleeves to the wrist and a skirt to the knee. Cloth over skin: fire reaches the cloth first.
A gold-shot band worn at the waist, over the robe.
Grey wool trousers, cut straight and ending where a boot begins. Nothing about them will turn an edge; they are what stands between your legs and the weather.
Cut leather, slow to catch. Better against a spill than against a fire.
A close iron helm with one slit across the eyes. Iron over the skull: fire finds nothing on it to catch, and acid pits it a grain at a time instead of eating it.

An iron breastplate with a gorget at the throat, a yoke across both shoulders, plate down each arm to the wrist and a short fauld over the hips. It does not burn. Acid takes it slowly, and a blade takes it not at all until it has beaten it in.
Iron cuisses and greaves, thigh to ankle. Heavy, fireproof, and slow to dissolve.
Iron shoes with an ankle cuff. What a spill of acid meets first, and what it gets through last.

Articulated iron over the back of each hand, with a cuff to the wrist. They will not stop much on their own; what they change is what your fists are for. A bare hand bruises. These cave a face in, a little at a time, and beat another man's plate while they do it.
A pull-over linen tunic, sleeves to the elbow and a body to mid-thigh, laced at the throat. What most people are wearing most of the time. It takes a dye evenly and it stops nothing.
A long working smock, full sleeves with cuffs and cloth enough in the skirt to move in. Mended once at the hem already; it will be mended again.
A sleeveless leather jerkin laced up the front, cut off at the waist. Bare shoulders, a bound armhole, and rather more between a blade and your ribs than linen manages.
Straight linen trousers, seamed down the outside of each leg and hemmed where a shoe begins.
Knee breeches, tied below the knee and leaving the calf to the weather. Worn with wraps, or with boots, or with nothing.
Close linen hose, gartered at the thigh and darned at one knee. Nothing about them is in the way, which is the only thing they have to recommend them.
Low leather shoes with a stitched sole and a lace across the instep. Better than bare feet on a road and worse than boots anywhere else.
Wooden clogs on a block sole, an inch of hardwood between you and the mud. They do not soak, they do not rot, and they burn like the log they were.
Strips of linen wound round the foot and crossed at the ankle. The cheapest thing that is not going barefoot, and the first thing to catch.

A stoppered glass flask. Hold the right button over any liquid to fill it, the left to pour it where you are looking. With the health panel open, a click on a limb pours it there -- over a wound, or a burn, or yourself.
A drawstring leather pouch for anything that pours but is not wet: sand, ash, dust, seed. Right button to scoop, left to scatter it where you look.
